newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia says will cut student cash as dissent grows.
newsitem.headline: Serbia says will cut student cash as dissent grows.

text.p: Opposition leaders vowed a long march to bring democracy to Serbia, but the socialist government lashed out at widening dissent by threatening to cut off cash for schools and universities.
"We have been here for more than 70 days...and we shall last 500 days," opposition politician Zoran Djindjic told cheering crowds in central Belgrade on Thursday night.
"Serbia has been ailing for half a century, and its healing will not be easy -- it will last a long time," he added.

In a terse report, the official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said the Serbian government, in a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic, decided that disruptions of some university, secondary and primary school classes violated several major laws.
"It decided to apply the law strictly against the offending establishments and withhold funds from them for the time they were not working," Tanjug reported.

It was not clear how speedily or effectively funds would be withheld, or the extent to which this would dent the zeal of the tens of thousands of Belgrade students spearheading daily protests, but the move drew a swift opposition response.
Vuk Draskovic, one of the leaders of the three-party opposition alliance, described the decision as disgraceful.
"We would not be surprised at all if the regime said tomorrow that opposition supporters' water supplies will be cut off," he told protesters on the 75th day of demonstrations.
Thursday's protests were distinctly boisterous despite the winter chill, with cars equipped with loudspeakers blaring gyspy music and fireworks bursting over the heads of a 50,000-strong crowd.
Many protesters, wrapped up in colourful scarves and woolly hats against the cold, sang, danced, drummed, whistled and cheered in a carnival atmosphere.
Only minor scuffles with police were reported as the huge gathering in a central Belgrade square finally broke up after a number of rousing political speeches.

Teachers have shut about 600 schools in a strike for better pay and conditions as well as educational reforms. Many university lecturers and professors have also turned out in support of student demands.

Serbia's autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic has stayed silent while dissent has widened. On Thursday Belgrade lawyers began a strike in sympathy with calls for Milosevic to recognise opposition victories in local elections.

Investigators from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have concluded that the November 17 polls, annulled by Milosevic's socialists on the grounds of "irregularities", were fair.

Both students, who choose to march through Belgrade's centre during the afternoon, and the opposition, which calls its supporters onto the streets after dark, share the demand that the opposition wins in 14 Serbian towns, including Belgrade, be fully recognised.
